title: Biggest Land Mass After One Fill
statement:
You get an n × n grid of 0 (water) and 1 (land). Land cells that touch up, down, left or right form one land mass, and its size is its number of cells.

You may turn at most one water cell into land. Return the size of the biggest land mass you can end up with.

examples.why: Filling the top middle cell joins the two top corners: 1 + 1 + 1. The centre cell touches no land at all, so filling it gives only 1.
There is no water to fill. The whole grid is already one mass.
The hole touches the same ring on all four sides. Count that ring once (8 cells) plus the filled cell, not 4 × 8 + 1.

hints: Filling a water cell merges itself with the land masses next to it. What do you need to know about those neighbours to get the new size instantly?
Label every land mass once with an id and store its size. Then a water cell's result is 1 plus the sizes of the masses around it.
A water cell can touch the same mass from several sides. Collect the distinct ids of its up to four neighbours before adding sizes. And if there is no water at all, the answer is n².

explain.intuition:
Trying every water cell and re-running a flood fill costs O(n²) per cell, O(n⁴) in total. The trick is to do the flood fills once. Paint every land mass with its own id and remember each id's size. Now filling a water cell joins only the masses that touch it directly, and you know their sizes by id.

So for each water cell, look at its four neighbours, collect the distinct ids, and add up their sizes plus one for the cell itself. The "distinct" part matters: a hole in the middle of a ring touches the same mass four times. The best over all water cells is the answer, unless there is no water, in which case the whole grid is land.
steps: Walk the grid. For each unlabelled land cell, flood fill it with a new id (starting at 2 so ids never clash with 0 and 1) and record the size in size[id].
Start best as the largest mass size found (covers grids with no water).
For each water cell, put the ids of its land neighbours into a small set.
Its candidate is 1 + sum of size[id] over that set. Update best.
pitfalls: Adding a neighbour's size once per side it touches. The ring in example 3 would count as 33 instead of 9.
Forgetting the all-land grid. There is no water cell to try, and the answer is n × n.
Recursive flood fill on a 500 × 500 grid can overflow the call stack in JavaScript and Python. Use an explicit stack or queue.

solutions.title: Fill each water cell and flood again
solutions.idea: For every water cell, pretend it is land and measure the mass it belongs to with a fresh search.

solutions.title: Label masses once, then score each water cell
solutions.idea: Flood fill every land mass with an id and store its size. A water cell scores 1 plus the sizes of the distinct ids around it.

followups: You may fill up to two water cells. Does the labelling idea still give a fast answer?
Cells are filled one at a time and you must report the biggest mass after each fill. Which structure handles the merging?
